title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 887–889 (Night 212, continuing nights-211), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 212 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. King Shahramān, sure that his son has been set upon and devoured by a wild beast or a highwayman, puts the Khālidān Islands into black, builds a House of Griefs, and spends all but two days a week there mourning him in verse. In the Ebony Islands, Budūr reigns as King Armānūs's supposed son-in-law and nightly laments her absent husband to Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, with verses of her own. Qamar al-Zamān, meanwhile, still weeps in the gardener's orchard waiting for the yearly ship; on a feast day, left alone, he falls, cuts his forehead on a tree, and then sees two birds fight until one tears off the other's head and flies away with it, and two great birds come down to mourn over the dead one, so that he weeps for his wife and his father; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the twelfth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and twelfth night,
sentences.n: al-thāniyata ʿashara, “twelfth”: as in the nights before, the print has عشر where Classical Arabic would make the second part feminine (ʿashrata) to agree with the night; it is vocalised as printed. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ لَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ إِنْشَادِهِ رَجَعَ بِجُيُوشِهِ إِلَى مَدِينَتِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika Shahramāna lammā faragha min inshādihi rajaʿa bi-juyūshihi ilā madīnatihi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that King Shahramān, when he-finished from his-reciting, returned with-his-armies to his-city,
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when King Shahramān had finished his recitation, he went back with his armies to his city.
sentences.n: The night takes up the last sentence of the one before. The print runs al-saʿīdu and anna together as one word, السعيدان; it is kept as set. Shahramāna is accusative after anna, a diptote with -a. faragha min, “to be done with”: min marks what is finished. rajaʿa bi-, “to go back with”: bi- marks those he takes along.

sentences.t: وَأَيْقَنَ بِهَلَاكِ وَلَدِهِ وَعَلِمَ أَنَّهُ عَدَى عَلَيْهِ وَافْتَرَسَهُ إِمَّا وَحْشٌ وَإِمَّا قَاطِعُ طَرِيقٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ayqana bi-halāki waladihi wa-ʿalima annahu ʿadā ʿalayhi wa-iftarasahu immā waḥshun wa-immā qāṭiʿu ṭarīqin
sentences.l: and-he-was-certain of-(the)-perishing (of) his-son, and-knew that-it-(was-that) set upon-him and-made-prey-of-him either a-wild-beast or a-cutter (of) road.
sentences.i: He was now certain that his son had perished, and knew that a wild beast or a highwayman must have fallen on him and made an end of him.
sentences.n: The print has على, a misprint for عدى, corrected here. ʿadā ʿalā, “to set upon, assault”: ʿalā marks the victim; the verb is written with ى for its final ā, as the print often writes it. ayqana bi-, Form IV, “to be certain of”: bi- marks what he is sure of. annahu: the -hu is the pronoun of the matter, “that (the case was that) …”, and the real subject comes after both verbs: immā … wa-immā …, “either … or …”. iftarasa, Form VIII, “to seize as prey, devour”, properly said of a beast of prey, here made to serve the highwayman too. qāṭiʿ ṭarīq, “cutter of the road”, a highwayman.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَادَى فِي جَزَائِرِ خَالِدَانَ أَنْ يَلْبَسُوا السَّوَادَ مِنَ الْأَحْزَانِ عَلَى وَلَدِهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma nādā fī jazāʾiri Khālidāna an yalbasū al-sawāda mina al-aḥzāni ʿalā waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: Then he-proclaimed in (the) islands (of) Khālidān that they-wear the-black from the-griefs over his-son Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: Then he had it proclaimed throughout the Islands of Khālidān that all should put on black in mourning for his son Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.n: nādā fī, Form III, “to proclaim, cry out in”: fī marks where the cry goes out. an yalbasū, subjunctive, “that they should wear”. al-sawād, “black”, the colour of mourning. min al-aḥzān, “out of griefs”: min gives the cause; ʿalā marks the one mourned. The clause rhymes aḥzān / zamān. Khālidāna is genitive, a diptote with -a. The ئ of جزائر is printed.

sentences.t: وَعَمِلَ لَهُ بَيْتًا وَسَمَّاهُ بَيْتَ الْأَحْزَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿamila lahu baytan wa-sammāhu bayta al-aḥzāni
sentences.l: And-he-made for-him a-house and-named-it (the) House (of) the-Griefs.
sentences.i: He set up a house for him and named it the House of Sorrows.
sentences.n: ʿamila, “to make”, here “to set up”; lahu, “for him”: li- marks the son, for whose sake it is made. sammā, Form II, “to name”, takes two objects, the thing and its name. bayt in the later language often means a room or chamber rather than a whole house.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ كُلَّ يَوْمِ خَمِيسٍ وَاثْنَيْنِ يَحْكُمُ فِي مَمْلَكَتِهِ بَيْنَ عَسْكَرِهِ وَرَعِيَّتِهِ وَبَقِيَّةَ الْجُمْعَةِ يَدْخُلُ إِلَى بَيْتِ الْحُزْنِ وَيَنْعَى عَلَى وَلَدِهِ وَيَرْثِيهِ بِالْأَشْعَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra kulla yawmi khamīsin wa-ithnayni yaḥkumu fī mamlakatihi bayna ʿaskarihi wa-raʿiyyatihi wa-baqiyyata al-jumʿati yadkhulu ilā bayti al-ḥuzni wa-yanʿā ʿalā waladihi wa-yarthīhi bi-al-ashʿāri
sentences.l: And-he-came, every day (of) Thursday and-Monday, (to) judge in his-kingdom between his-army and-his-subjects, and-(the)-rest (of) the-week (to) go into (the) House (of) the-Grief and-bewail over his-son and-elegize-him with-the-poems.
sentences.i: Every Thursday and Monday he would sit in judgement in his kingdom among his soldiers and his subjects, and the rest of the week he would go into the House of Grief, bewail his son and lament him in verse.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “he came to do”, of a settled habit. kulla yawmi khamīsin wa-ithnayni, “every Thursday and Monday”, an accusative of time: yawm al-khamīs, “the fifth day”, is Thursday, and yawm al-ithnayn, “the second day”, Monday; here both stand without the article. baqiyyata al-jumʿati, “the rest of the week”, is likewise an accusative of time: al-jumʿa, properly “Friday”, means the whole week here, as in the spoken Arabic. The House of “Griefs” has become the House of “Grief”, bayt al-ḥuzn. naʿā ʿalā, “to bewail”: classically naʿā means “to announce a death”; ʿalā marking the one mourned is the later usage. rathā, “to lament in an elegy”: bi- marks the means.

sentences.t: فَمِنْ ذٰلِكَ قَوْلُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-min dhālika qawluhu
sentences.l: And-of that (is) his-saying:
sentences.i: Among these laments are his words:
sentences.n: fa-min dhālika qawluhu, “and of that is his saying”, the narrator's way of giving one sample among many.

sentences.t:
فَيَوْمُ الْاَمَانِيْ يَوْمَ قُرْبِكُمْ مِنِّيْ * وَيَوْمُ الْمَنَايَا يَوْمَ اِعْرَاضِكُمْ عَنِّيْ
اِذَا بِتُّ مَرْعُوبًا اُهَدَّدُ بِالرَّدَى * فَوَصْلُكُمُ عِنْدِيْ اَلَذُّ مِنَ الْاَمْنِ
sentences.tr:
fa-yawmu al-amānī yawma qurbikum minnī * wa-yawmu al-manāyā yawma iʿrāḍikum ʿannī
idhā bittu marʿūban uhaddadu bi-al-radā * fa-waṣlukumu ʿindī aladhdhu mina al-amni
sentences.l:
For-(the)-day (of) the-hopes (is the) day (of) your-nearness to-me, * and-(the)-day (of) the-deaths (the) day (of) your-turning-away from-me.
When I-spend-the-night terrified, being-threatened with-the-destruction, * then-union-with-you with-me (is) sweeter than the-safety.
sentences.i:
The day of all my hopes is the day you are near me, * and the day of my death the day you turn away from me.
When I pass the night in terror, with ruin threatening, * your company is sweeter to me than safety.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The father speaks to his lost son in the plural, -kum, “you”, as poets address the beloved. amānī, plural of umniyya, “hope, wish”, plays against manāyā, plural of maniyya, “death, fate”: the two words are made of almost the same letters. The print points yawma, accusative, in both hemistichs: “the day of hopes is (on) the day of your nearness”. iʿrāḍ ʿan, Form IV, “turning away from”: ʿan marks the one turned from. bittu, “I spent the night”, from bāta. uhaddadu, passive of Form II haddada, “to threaten”: bi- marks the threat; radā, “destruction, death”. waṣl, “union, the beloved's company”; waṣlukumu keeps an old long -u on the pronoun for the metre. ʿindī, “with me”, that is, in my eyes. aladhdhu min, “sweeter than”: min marks the thing compared. The print writes a bare alif without hamza in اَلْاَمَانِيْ, اِعْرَاضِكُمْ, اِذَا, اُهَدَّدُ, اَلَذُّ and الْاَمْنِ, and a sukūn on many long vowels; all are kept.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ ذٰلِكَ قَوْلُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-min dhālika qawluhu
sentences.l: And-of that (is) his-saying:
sentences.i: And these words too are his:

sentences.t:
نَفْسِى الْفِدَاءُ لِظَاعِنِيْنَ رَحِيْلُهُمْ * اَنْكَى وَاَفْسَدَ فِى الْقُلُوْبِ وَعَاثَا
فَلْيَقْضِ عِدَّتَهُ السُّرُوْرُ فَاِنَّنِيْ * طَلَّقْتُ بَعْدَهُمُ النَّعِيْمَ ثَلَاثَا
sentences.tr:
nafsī al-fidāʾu li-ẓāʿinīna raḥīluhum * ankā wa-afsada fī al-qulūbi wa-ʿāthā
fa-l-yaqḍi ʿiddatahu al-surūru fa-innanī * ṭallaqtu baʿdahumu al-naʿīma thalāthā
sentences.l:
My-soul (is) the-ransom for-departing-ones whose-departure * wounded and-spoiled in the-hearts and-wrought-havoc.
So-let-complete its-waiting-period the-joy, for-indeed-I * have-divorced after-them the-ease three-(times).
sentences.i:
My life be ransom for the travellers whose leaving * has wounded, spoiled and laid waste the heart!
Let joy now see out its waiting-term, for I * have divorced delight three times since they went.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is kāmil, and the lines rhyme in -āthā. nafsī al-fidāʾu li-, “my soul is the ransom for”, that is, I would give my life for: li- marks those ransomed. ẓāʿinūn, “those setting out”, the poets' word for the beloved's people breaking camp. ankā, Form IV, “to wound, inflict harm”; afsada, Form IV, “to spoil, corrupt”; ʿāthā, “wrought havoc”, ʿātha with the alif that lengthens the rhyme. The second line is a legal conceit: a man who has divorced his wife three times may not take her back, and a divorced woman keeps a waiting period, ʿidda, before she may marry again. The poet has divorced naʿīm, “ease, delight”, beyond recall, and tells surūr, “joy”, to see out its waiting period, for there is no return. fa-l-yaqḍi, “so let (it) fulfil”, li- of command with the jussive. ṭallaqa, Form II, “to divorce”. baʿdahumu, “after them”, with the long -u of the pronoun for the metre. thalāthā, “three (times)”, for thalāthan, its alif kept for the rhyme. The print writes a bare alif without hamza in اَنْكَى, وَاَفْسَدَ and فَاِنَّنِيْ, and ى for final ī in نَفْسِى and فِى; all are kept.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri al-maliki Shahramāna
sentences.l: This (is) what was of (the) affair (of) King Shahramān.
sentences.i: So much for King Shahramān.
sentences.n: hādhā mā kāna min amri …, “this is what there was of the affair of …”, the narrator's formula for leaving one strand of the tale for another. Shahramāna is genitive, a diptote with -a.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ بِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ فَإِنَّهَا صَارَتْ مَلِكَةً فِي بِلَادِ الْآبَنُوسِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-malikati Budūra binti al-maliki al-Ghayūri fa-innahā ṣārat malikatan fī bilādi al-Ābanūsi
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) the-Queen Budūr, daughter (of) King al-Ghayūr, indeed-she became queen in (the) lands (of) the-Ebony.
sentences.i: As for Queen Budūr, daughter of King al-Ghayūr, she had become sovereign in the land of Ebony.
sentences.n: wa-ammā … fa-innahā, “as for …, she …”. Budūra is genitive, a diptote with -a, and binti stands in apposition to it. bilād al-Ābanūs, “the lands of Ebony”, the kingdom of King Armānūs, where Budūr, in her husband's clothes, has been made king in his place; the narrator calls her malika, “queen”, though the people take her for a man. The madda of الآبنوس is printed.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ النَّاسُ يُشِيرُونَ إِلَيْهَا بِالْبَنَانِ وَيَقُولُونَ هٰذَا صِهْرُ الْمَلِكِ أَرْمَانُوسَ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra al-nāsu yushīrūna ilayhā bi-al-banāni wa-yaqūlūna hādhā ṣihru al-maliki Armānūsa
sentences.l: And-came the-people (to) point to-her with-the-fingertips and-say: This (is the) son-in-law (of) King Armānūs.
sentences.i: People would point her out to one another and say, “That is King Armānūs's son-in-law.”
sentences.n: ashāra ilā … bi-, Form IV, “to point at with”: ilā marks the one pointed at, bi- the finger; yushāru ilayhi bi-al-banān, “he is pointed at with the fingertips”, is the set phrase for someone famous. ṣihr, “son-in-law”: they take her for the young man who married the king's daughter. Armānūsa is genitive, a diptote with -a.

sentences.t: وَكُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ تَنَامُ مَعَ السِّتِّ حَيٰوةِ النُّفُوسِ وَتَشْتَكِي وَحْشَةَ زَوْجِهَا قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-kulla laylatin tanāmu maʿa al-sitti Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi wa-tashtakī waḥshata zawjihā Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-every night she-sleeps with the-Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs and-complains (of the) desolation (of) her-husband Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: Every night she slept beside the Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs and poured out how she missed her husband Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.n: kulla laylatin, “every night”, an accusative of time. al-sitt, “the Lady”, the spoken word for sayyida. Ḥayāt is printed حيٰوة, the old spelling with wāw and a dagger alif; it is kept. ishtakā, Form VIII, “to complain of”, takes its object directly. waḥsha, “desolation, the loneliness of absence”: waḥshat zawjihā, “the loneliness of (missing) her husband”.

sentences.t: وَهِيَ تَبْكِي وَتَصِفُ لِحَيٰوةِ النُّفُوسِ حُسْنَهُ وَجَمَالَهُ وَتَتَمَنَّى وَلَوْفِى الْمَنَامِ وِصَالَهُ وَتُنْشِدُ وَتَقُولُ
sentences.tr: wa-hiya tabkī wa-taṣifu li-Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi ḥusnahu wa-jamālahu wa-tatamannā wa-law fī al-manāmi wiṣālahu wa-tunshidu wa-taqūlu
sentences.l: And-she weeps and-describes to-Ḥayāt al-Nufūs his-beauty and-his-loveliness, and-wishes, even-if in the-sleep, his-union, and-recites and-says:
sentences.i: She would weep as she described his beauty and grace to Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, longing to be united with him, if only in a dream; and she would recite:
sentences.n: wa-hiya tabkī, “she weeping”, a circumstantial clause. waṣafa li-, “to describe to”: li- marks the listener. tamannā, Form V, “to long for”. wa-law, “even if (only)”; the print sets wa-law fī as one word, ولوفى, and it is kept as set. wiṣāl, “union with the beloved”. The clause rhymes jamālahu / wiṣālahu. tunshidu wa-taqūlu, “recites and says”, introduces the verse.

sentences.t:
اَللّٰهُ اَعْلَمُ اِنِّيْ بَعْدَ فُرْقَتِكُمْ * بَكَيْتُ حَتَّى اِسْتَلَفْتُ الدَّمْعَ بِالدَّيْنِ
وَقَالَ لِيْ عَاذِلِيْ اِصْبِرْ تَنَالُهُمْ * فَقُلْتُ يَا عَاذِلِيْ اَلصَّبْرُ مِنْ اَيْنِ
sentences.tr:
Allāhu aʿlamu innī baʿda furqatikum * bakaytu ḥattā istalaftu al-damʿa bi-al-dayni
wa-qāla lī ʿādhilī iṣbir tanāluhum * fa-qultu yā ʿādhilī al-ṣabru min ayni
sentences.l:
God knows: I, after your-parting, * wept until I-borrowed the-tears on-the-credit.
And-said to-me my-blamer: Be-patient, you-will-attain-them; * and-I-said: O my-blamer, the-patience — from where?
sentences.i:
God knows that since you parted from me * I have wept until I had to borrow tears on credit.
My critic said to me, “Be patient, and you will have them back.” * I said, “My critic, and where am I to find patience?”
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is basīṭ, and the lines rhyme in -ayni. Budūr speaks to her absent husband in the plural, -kum, as poets address the beloved. The print points innī with kasra after aʿlamu, where Classical grammar would want annī, “that I”; it reads as “God knows: I …”. furqa, “parting”. istalafa, Form VIII, “to borrow”: bi-al-dayni, “on credit”, bi- marks the terms; her own tears are spent, so she weeps with borrowed ones. ʿādhil, “the blamer”, the stock figure who rebukes a lover. tanāluhum, “you will obtain them”: after an imperative Classical grammar wants the jussive, tanalhum; the print points the indicative, and it is kept. min ayni, “from where?”: ayna is pointed ayni for the rhyme with dayni. The print writes a bare alif without hamza in اَعْلَمُ, اِنِّيْ, اِصْبِرْ and اَيْنِ, and puts vowels on the alif of joining in اِسْتَلَفْتُ, اِصْبِرْ and اَلصَّبْرُ; all are kept.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri al-malikati Budūra
sentences.l: This (is) what was of (the) affair (of) the-Queen Budūr.
sentences.i: So much for Queen Budūr.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فَإِنَّهُ أَقَامَ عِنْدَ الْخَوْلِيِّ فِى الْبُسْتَانِ مُدَّةً مِنَ الزَّمَانِ وَهُوَ يَبْكِي بِاللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ وَيُنْشِدُ الْأَشْعَارَ وَيَتَحَسَّرُ عَلَى أَوْقَاتِ الْهَنَا وَلَيَالِي الْمُنَا
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri Qamari al-Zamāni fa-innahu aqāma ʿinda al-khawliyyi fī al-bustāni muddatan mina al-zamāni wa-huwa yabkī bi-al-layli wa-al-nahāri wa-yunshidu al-ashʿāra wa-yataḥassaru ʿalā awqāti al-hanā wa-layālī al-munā
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) Qamar al-Zamān, indeed-he stayed with the-gardener in the-garden a-space of the-time, and-he weeping by-the-night and-the-day, and-reciting the-poems, and-sighing over (the) times (of) the-happiness and-(the)-nights (of) the-wishes.
sentences.i: As for Qamar al-Zamān, he stayed on with the gardener in the orchard for some time, weeping night and day, reciting verses, and sighing for the days of happiness and the nights of fulfilled desire.
sentences.n: aqāma ʿinda, Form IV, “to stay with”: ʿinda marks the host. khawlī, “gardener, keeper of an orchard”, an Egyptian word. muddatan mina al-zamāni, “a space of time”. bi-al-layli wa-al-nahāri, “by night and day”: bi- marks the time. taḥassara ʿalā, Form V, “to sigh with regret for”: ʿalā marks what is lost; its shadda is printed. al-hanā, “happiness, ease”, is hanāʾ without its hamza, and al-munā, “wishes”, plural of munya, is written with alif for ى; the two rhyme, as nahār does with ashʿār.

sentences.t: وَالْخَوْلِيُّ يَقُولُ لَهُ فِي آخِرِ السَّنَةِ تَسِيرُ الْمَرْكَبُ إِلَى بِلَادِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-al-khawliyyu yaqūlu lahu fī ākhiri al-sanati tasīru al-markabu ilā bilādi al-muslimīna
sentences.l: And-the-gardener says to-him: In (the) end (of) the-year sails the-ship to (the) lands (of) the-Muslims.
sentences.i: And the gardener would tell him, “At the end of the year the ship sails for the lands of the Muslims.”
sentences.n: yaqūlu, imperfect: he said it again and again. markab, “ship”, is masculine in Classical Arabic; here it takes the feminine verb tasīru, as in the spoken language. The madda of آخر is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ إِلَى أَنْ رَآى النَّاسَ مُجْتَمِعِينَ عَلَى بَعْضِهِمْ فَتَعَجَّبَ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal Qamaru al-Zamāni ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati ilā an raʾā al-nāsa mujtamiʿīna ʿalā baʿḍihim fa-taʿajjaba min dhālika
sentences.l: And-not ceased Qamar al-Zamān upon that the-state until that he-saw the-people gathered upon each-other, and-he-wondered at that.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān went on in this state until one day he saw people gathering together, and wondered at it.
sentences.n: lam yazal … ʿalā, “did not cease to be in (a state)”: ʿalā marks the state. ilā an, “until”, here with the perfect. raʾā is printed رآى, with a madda and a final yāʾ, a spelling of the later language; it is kept. mujtamiʿīna ʿalā baʿḍihim, “gathered on one another”, crowding together, a spoken turn. taʿajjaba min, Form V, “to wonder at”: min marks the cause.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهِ الْخَوْلِيُّ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي بَطِّلِ الشُّغْلَ فِي هٰذَا الْيَوْمِ وَلَا تُحَوِّلِ الْمَاءَ إِلَى الْأَشْجَارِ لِأَنَّ هٰذَا الْيَوْمَ عِيدٌ وَالنَّاسُ فِيهِ يَزُورُ بَعْضُهُمْ بَعْضًا
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala ʿalayhi al-khawliyyu wa-qāla lahu yā waladī baṭṭili al-shughla fī hādhā al-yawmi wa-lā tuḥawwili al-māʾa ilā al-ashjāri li-anna hādhā al-yawma ʿīdun wa-al-nāsu fīhi yazūru baʿḍuhum baʿḍan
sentences.l: And-came-in upon-him the-gardener and-said to-him: O my-son, stop the-work in this the-day, and-do-not turn the-water to the-trees, because this the-day (is) a-feast, and-the-people, in-it visits some-of-them some.
sentences.i: Then the gardener came in to him and said, “My son, leave off work today, and do not turn the water on to the trees, for today is a feast day, when people go visiting one another.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, “to come in to”: ʿalā marks the person visited. baṭṭil, imperative of Form II baṭṭala, “to stop, leave off”, a word of the later language; the print marks its kasra and shadda, and the final -i is a joining vowel before al-. ḥawwala … ilā, Form II, “to turn (water) to”: ilā marks where it is led, along the little channels of the irrigated garden; its shadda is printed. li-anna, “because”. yazūru baʿḍuhum baʿḍan, “some of them visit others”, that is, they visit one another: the verb is singular, agreeing with baʿḍ, though the people are many. The hamza of الماء is printed.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَرِحْ وَاجْعَلْ بَالَكَ إِلَى الْغَيْطِ فَإِنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُبْصِرَ لَكَ مَرْكَبًا فَمَا بَقِيَ إِلَّا الْقَلِيلُ وَأُرْسِلُكَ إِلَى بِلَادِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-istariḥ wa-ijʿal bālaka ilā al-ghayṭi fa-innī urīdu an ubṣira laka markaban fa-mā baqiya illā al-qalīlu wa-ursiluka ilā bilādi al-muslimīna
sentences.l: So-rest, and-put your-mind to the-field, for-indeed-I want that I-look-out for-you a-ship; for-not remained except the-little, and-I-send-you to (the) lands (of) the-Muslims.
sentences.i: So rest, and keep an eye on the field, for I mean to find you a ship. It will not be long now, and then I shall send you off to the lands of the Muslims.”
sentences.n: istarāḥa, Form X, “to rest”. ijʿal bālaka ilā, “put your mind to”, keep watch over: ilā marks what he is to mind. bāl, “mind, attention”, and ghayṭ, “field”, are everyday words of the later language. abṣara li-, Form IV, “to look out (something) for”: li- marks the one it is for, a spoken usage. fa-mā baqiya illā al-qalīlu, “only a little (time) is left”. ursiluka, indicative, “and (then) I will send you”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْخَوْلِيَّ خَرَجَ مِنَ الْبُسْتَانِ وَبَقِيَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَحْدَهُ وَتَفَكَّرَ فِي حَالِهِ فَانْكَسَرَ خَاطِرُهُ وَجَرَتْ دُمُوعُهُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-khawliyya kharaja mina al-bustāni wa-baqiya Qamaru al-Zamāni waḥdahu wa-tafakkara fī ḥālihi fa-inkasara khāṭiruhu wa-jarat dumūʿuhu
sentences.l: Then indeed the-gardener went-out from the-garden, and-remained Qamar al-Zamān (in) his-aloneness, and-he-reflected on his-state, and-was-broken his-mind, and-ran his-tears.
sentences.i: Then the gardener went out of the orchard, and Qamar al-Zamān was left alone. He thought over his plight; his heart broke, and his tears flowed.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”, the narrator's turn to the next event: al-khawliyya is accusative after inna. waḥdahu, “by himself”, an adverbial accusative. tafakkara fī, Form V, “to reflect on”: fī marks the subject of his thoughts. inkasara khāṭiruhu, “his mind was broken”, he was heartbroken: khāṭir, “mind, feelings”, in the later language.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ بَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا حَتَّى غُشِيَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni bakā bukāʾan shadīdan ḥattā ghushiya ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān wept a-weeping violent, until it-was-covered over-him.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān wept so bitterly that he fainted.
sentences.n: bukāʾan shadīdan, “a violent weeping”, an absolute object that gives the verb its force. ghushiya ʿalayhi, “he fainted”, literally “it was covered over him”: the passive is impersonal, and ʿalā marks the one who swoons. The hamza of بكاء is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَ قَامَ يَتَمَشَّى فِى الْبُسْتَانِ وَهُوَ مُتَفَكِّرٌ فِيمَا فَعَلَ فِيهِ الزَّمَانُ وَطُولُ الْبُعْدِ وَالْهِجْرَانُ غَائِبَ الْعَقْلِ وَلْهَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afāqa qāma yatamashshā fī al-bustāni wa-huwa mutafakkirun fīmā faʿala fīhi al-zamānu wa-ṭūlu al-buʿdi wa-al-hijrānu ghāʾiba al-ʿaqli walhāna
sentences.l: And-when he-came-to, he-rose walking-about in the-garden, and-he (was) reflecting on-what had-done to-him the-time and-(the)-length (of) the-distance and-the-forsaking, absent (of) the-mind, distraught.
sentences.i: When he came to himself he got up and wandered about the orchard, brooding on what fortune had done to him, and the long distance and separation; his wits had left him, and he was beside himself with grief.
sentences.n: afāqa, Form IV, “to come to, recover one's senses”. qāma yatamashshā, “he rose, walking about”: tamashshā, Form V, “to stroll, walk about”. mutafakkir fī, “reflecting on”: fī marks the subject of his thoughts; its shadda is printed. fīmā is fī mā, “on what”. faʿala fīhi, “did to him”: fī marks the one acted upon. al-zamān, “time”, here fortune, has two more subjects beside it, ṭūl al-buʿd, “the length of distance”, and al-hijrān, “forsaking, separation”; the prose rhymes al-zamān / al-hijrān / walhān. ghāʾiba al-ʿaqli, “absent of mind”, and walhān, “distraught with grief”, describe his state: both accusative, walhān without tanwīn, as words of the faʿlān pattern are. The ئ of غائب is printed.

sentences.t: فَعَثَرَ فَوَقَعَ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ فَجَاءَتْ جَبْهَتُهُ عَلَى جِدْرِ شَجَرَةٍ فَبَطَّتْهُ وَجَرَى مِنْهُ الدَّمُ وَاخْتَلَطَ بِدُمُوعِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿathara fa-waqaʿa ʿalā wajhihi fa-jāʾat jabhatuhu ʿalā jidri shajaratin fa-baṭṭat-hu wa-jarā minhu al-damu wa-ikhtalaṭa bi-dumūʿihi
sentences.l: And-he-stumbled and-fell on his-face, and-came his-forehead upon (the) root (of) a-tree, and-it-slit-it, and-ran from-it the-blood and-mingled with-his-tears.
sentences.i: He stumbled and fell on his face; his forehead struck the root of a tree and was split open, and the blood ran from it and mingled with his tears.
sentences.n: jāʾat jabhatuhu ʿalā, “his forehead came upon”, it struck. The print has جدر, which we vocalise jidr and read as “root, stump”: it may be meant for jidhr (جذر), the Classical word, which the spoken language says with d; the reading is likely but not certain. baṭṭa, “to slit, lance”, as one opens a swelling: the feminine verb has the tree or the forehead for subject, and -hu loosely stands for him or his brow; the sense, that the brow was laid open, is clear. jarā min, “to flow from”: min marks the source. ikhtalaṭa bi-, Form VIII, “to mingle with”: bi- marks what it mixes with. The hamza of جاءت is printed.

sentences.t: فَمَسَحَ دَمَهُ وَنَشَّفَ دُمُوعَهُ وَشَدَّ جَبْهَتَهُ بِخِرْقَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-masaḥa damahu wa-nashshafa dumūʿahu wa-shadda jabhatahu bi-khirqatin
sentences.l: And-he-wiped his-blood and-dried his-tears and-bound his-forehead with-a-rag.
sentences.i: He wiped away the blood, dried his tears, and bound up his forehead with a strip of cloth.
sentences.n: nashshafa, Form II, “to dry (something)”: we point the Form II, since Form I nashifa means “to dry up” of itself. shadda bi-, “to bind with”: bi- marks the means; the shadda of وشدّ is printed. khirqa, “rag, strip of cloth”.

sentences.t: وَقَامَ يَتَمَشَّى فِي ذٰلِكَ الْبُسْتَانِ وَهُوَ فِي فِكْرِهِ ذَاهِلُ الْعَقْلِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāma yatamashshā fī dhālika al-bustāni wa-huwa fī fikrihi dhāhilu al-ʿaqli
sentences.l: And-he-rose walking-about in that the-garden, and-he (was) in his-thought, dazed (of) the-mind.
sentences.i: Then he got up and walked about the orchard once more, lost in thought, his mind dazed.
sentences.n: wa-huwa fī fikrihi, “he being in his thought”, a circumstantial clause; dhāhilu al-ʿaqli, “dazed of mind”, is a second predicate of huwa.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ بِعَيْنِهِ إِلَى شَجَرَةٍ فَوْقَهَا طَائِرَانِ يَتَخَاصَمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara bi-ʿaynihi ilā shajaratin fawqahā ṭāʾirāni yatakhāṣamāni
sentences.l: And-he-looked with-his-eye to a-tree, above-it two-birds quarrelling-with-each-other.
sentences.i: His eye fell on a tree in which two birds were fighting.
sentences.n: naẓara bi-ʿaynihi ilā, “looked with his eye at”: bi- marks the means, ilā what is looked at. fawqahā ṭāʾirāni, “above it (were) two birds”, a clause describing the tree. takhāṣama, Form VI, “to quarrel with one another”, here dual. The ئ of طائران is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ أَحَدُهُمَا إِلَى الْآخَرِ وَنَقَرَهُ فِي رَقَبَتِهِ فَخَلَّصَهَا مِنْ جُثَّتِهِ وَأَخَذَ رَأْسَهُ وَطَارَ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma aḥaduhumā ilā al-ākhari wa-naqarahu fī raqabatihi fa-khallaṣahā min juththatihi wa-akhadha raʾsahu wa-ṭāra bihi
sentences.l: And-rose one-of-them to the-other and-pecked-him in his-neck, and-severed-it from his-body, and-took his-head and-flew with-it.
sentences.i: One of them went for the other and pecked him in the neck until it came away from his body; then he took the head and flew off with it.
sentences.n: qāma ilā, “to rise against, go for”: ilā marks the one attacked. naqara fī, “to peck at”: fī marks where the beak strikes. khallaṣa min, Form II, “to free from, detach from”: here, he cut the neck clean from the body. ṭāra bi-, “to fly off with”: bi- marks what is carried. The madda of الآخر and the hamza of رأسه are printed.

sentences.t: وَوَقَعَ الْمَقْتُولُ فِى الْأَرْضِ قُدَّامَ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-waqaʿa al-maqtūlu fī al-arḍi quddāma Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-fell the-slain-one in the-ground before Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: The dead bird fell to the ground in front of Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.n: al-maqtūl, “the slain one”, the passive participle of qatala. waqaʿa fī al-arḍi, “fell to the ground”: fī, “on”, where Classical Arabic would more often say ʿalā. quddāma, “in front of”.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ كَذٰلِكَ وَإِذَا بِطَائِرَيْنِ كَبِيرَيْنِ قَدِ انْقَضَّا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa ka-dhālika wa-idhā bi-ṭāʾirayni kabīrayni qadi inqaḍḍā ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And-while he (was) like-that, and-behold, two-birds big had swooped upon-it.
sentences.i: While he stood there, all at once two large birds swooped down on it.
sentences.n: baynamā … wa-idhā, “while … behold”: idhā marks the sudden sight, and the bi- after it only marks what appears. inqaḍḍa ʿalā, Form VII, “to swoop down on”, of a bird: ʿalā marks what is swooped on, here the dead bird; the shadda of انقضّا is printed, and the verb is dual. qadi is qad with a joining kasra. The ئ of بطائرين is printed.

sentences.t: وَوَقَفَ أَحَدُهُمَا عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ وَالْآخَرُ عِنْدَ ذَنَبِهِ وَأَرْخَيَا أَجْنِحَتَهُمَا وَمَنَاقِيرَهُمَا عَلَيْهِ وَمَدَّا أَعْنَاقَهُمَا إِلَيْهِ وَبَكَيَا
sentences.tr: wa-waqafa aḥaduhumā ʿinda raʾsihi wa-al-ākharu ʿinda dhanabihi wa-arkhayā ajniḥatahumā wa-manāqīrahumā ʿalayhi wa-maddā aʿnāqahumā ilayhi wa-bakayā
sentences.l: And-stood one-of-them at its-head and-the-other at its-tail, and-they-two-let-down their-wings and-their-beaks over-it, and-they-two-stretched their-necks to-it, and-they-two-wept.
sentences.i: One of them stood at its head and the other at its tail; they let their wings and beaks droop over it, stretched their necks towards it, and wept.
sentences.n: The verbs after the first are dual, -ā, “the two of them”. arkhā, Form IV, “to let hang, lower”: ʿalā, “over”, marks what they bend over. manāqīr, plural of minqār, “beak”. madda ilā, “to stretch towards”: ilā marks the direction; the shadda of ومدّا is printed. ajniḥa, plural of janāḥ, “wing”; aʿnāq, plural of ʿunuq, “neck”. The madda of والآخر and the hamza of رأسه are printed.

sentences.t: فَبَكَى قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ عَلَى فِرَاقِ زَوْجَتِهِ وَتَذَكَّرَ وَالِدَةُ حِينَ رَأَى الطَّائِرَيْنِ يَبْكِيَانِ عَلَى صَاحِبِهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-bakā Qamaru al-Zamāni ʿalā firāqi zawjatihi wa-tadhakkara wālidahu ḥīna raʾā al-ṭāʾirayni yabkiyāni ʿalā ṣāḥibihimā
sentences.l: And-wept Qamar al-Zamān over (the) parting (of) his-wife, and-remembered his-father, when he-saw the-two-birds weeping over their-companion.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān wept for the loss of his wife, and remembered his father, as he watched the two birds weeping over their companion.
sentences.n: bakā ʿalā, “to weep over”: ʿalā marks what is mourned. tadhakkara, Form V, “to remember”; its shadda is printed. The print has والدة, which would ordinarily be wālida, “mother”; here it is read wālidahu, “his father”, the ة standing for the pronoun -hu, as the print writes it elsewhere in this tale; the dāl takes the fatḥa of the object of tadhakkara. ṣāḥib, “companion”. raʾā is printed here with hamza, رأى, where above it was رآى; the ئ of الطائرين is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print sets the name as two words, شهر زاد; they are kept as set.
